sentences.text: The editor requested that page fourteen end mid-gesture, so the turn lands on the empty apartment splash. Grandma's dishes won't survive a storage unit, and the unit costs more monthly than they're worth anyway. Panel three repeats panel one exactly, except the coffee has gone cold and her phone screen is dark. Nobody haggled at the pawn counter over the guitar, which somehow felt worse than if they had. Our colorist keyed the chapter to a bruise palette, then stripped every warm tone except the stairwell bulb. Overtime used to be a choice; now I take every shift posted and it still doesn't touch the arrears. Honestly, the bravest choice in the whole issue is the double-page spread of nothing but her ceiling. Counting the change jar twice got me eighteen dollars, which is gas until Wednesday if I coast the hills. Do we really need dialogue at the bus stop, or can the sodium lights do the talking? Called my sister at lunch; her silence cost me more than the rent I was asking about. Print tests came back too dark; the press flattened the blue washes that carry the entire mood. A thumbs-up from my cousin about borrowing his truck; that tiny icon is holding the whole moving day together. Around page nine we swapped her font for a thinner cut, and readers felt it without knowing why. Some nights I lay the bills out across the table like a hand of cards nobody would bet on. Give me nine panels here, all the same size — the grid does the suffocating for us. Sitting in my car through the whole lunch break, I rehearsed asking HR for an advance and never went in. A 2-4-2 tier structure holds until the dream sequence, where the borders dissolve into torn-paper edges. Rent, then electric, then the minimum on the card — some sequence of those three, never all of them. "Silent page," Mara scrawled across the thumbnail, then underlined it twice in red. Somebody at work joked about vacation plans and I laughed with a mouth full of vending-machine crackers. I want to write a suicide letter.
